opus-5.5.text:
I think the value is quite fundamental, and it comes from a simple observation: the world we live in is three-dimensional, and if we want AI systems that can actually act in that world, not just talk about it, they need some internal representation that respects its structure.

Language models have been incredibly successful because they've learned a compressed model of human knowledge expressed through text. But text is a very lossy description of physical reality. If you want a robot to pick up a cup, or a car to navigate an intersection, you need to understand geometry, occlusion, how objects move, how light interacts with surfaces, what happens when you push something. That's what I mean by a world model: a system that can predict how the world evolves, especially in response to actions.

Now, there's a debate about whether you need explicit 3D reconstruction or whether a model can learn implicitly from video. My view is that both are useful, and they complement each other. Video generation models have shown surprising emergent 3D consistency, which tells us that a lot of physical structure can be learned from pixels at scale. But explicit 3D reconstruction gives you things that are very hard to get otherwise. It gives you persistence: if you walk around a room and come back, the table is still there and looks the same. It gives you controllability: you can place a camera anywhere, change the lighting, move objects around. And it gives you a form of grounding you can measure and verify, which matters a lot when you're training robots or validating autonomous vehicles.

From a practical standpoint, one of the biggest bottlenecks in physical AI is data. Collecting real-world robot data is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. If you can reconstruct real environments in 3D and then generate variations, different layouts, different weather, different edge cases, you essentially turn the world into a simulator you can scale. That's where I see a lot of near-term value: synthetic data generation, policy evaluation, and closing the gap between simulation and reality.

Longer term, I think the most interesting direction is unifying these ideas: a world model that can perceive the 3D structure of a scene, reason about it, imagine what happens next, and render that imagination back out as something we can see and use. That's a big part of why we've been working on platforms like Cosmos at NVIDIA. The goal is to give the physical AI community foundation models for the physical world, the way language foundation models changed NLP.

So in short, reconstructing the 3D world isn't the end goal by itself. It's a way of giving AI a more faithful, controllable, and scalable understanding of reality, and I think that's a prerequisite for AI that really works in the physical world.

fable-5.1.text:
Ming-Yu Liu: I think the honest way to say it is that the world is three-dimensional, and anything that has to act in it needs to understand that. A language model lives in text. A video model, in some sense, lives in a sequence of two-dimensional pictures. But a robot, a car, a drone, they don't experience the world as pictures. They move through space, they bump into things, they pick objects up and put them down. So if you want a model that is useful for a physical agent, it has to carry some notion of space, of geometry, of what is behind the thing in front of it.

Now, there's a debate about whether you need to reconstruct that geometry explicitly, or whether a model can learn it implicitly just by predicting what the next frame looks like. My view is that both are valuable, and they serve different purposes. If you only predict pixels, the model may learn a lot about physics and appearance, but it can be very hard to check whether it actually got the world right. The video can look beautiful and still be wrong about where the table is. When a model can produce a three-dimensional representation, you get something you can measure. You can ask, is this object really 30 centimeters away, is the floor flat, does the hand actually reach the cup. That matters a lot when a mistake has a cost in the real world.

The second value is consistency. A real environment doesn't change when you turn your head. If I look left and then look back, the chair should still be there. Models that reason purely in images struggle with that kind of persistence. A three-dimensional world model gives you memory of the scene almost for free. That's what makes it useful for long-horizon planning, for navigation, for anything where the agent has to return to a place it has seen before.

And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is data. Collecting real robot data is slow and expensive. If you can reconstruct a scene in three dimensions, you can generate many variations of it. Change the lighting, move the objects, put the camera somewhere else, and now you have training data that is physically grounded rather than invented from nothing. So a world model that understands three-dimensional structure isn't only a model for perception. It becomes a simulator, and simulators are how we get physical AI to scale.

So, to summarize, I'd say the value is verifiability, consistency, and scale. Those are the three things you need before you trust a model to control something that can actually break.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is that a three-dimensional world model gives an AI system a representation of how things relate in space. Where are the objects? What is behind them? If I move to another position, what should I see? Those are important questions for an agent that needs to interact with the physical world.

But reconstruction is only part of the story. You also want to understand how the world changes when you take an action. If a robot pushes an object, where will it go? Can the robot predict that before actually doing it? A world model that supports those predictions could be useful for planning and for training robots in simulation.

So, to me, the exciting thing is connecting perception to action. You’re building a representation that can help a system decide what to do next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is that a three-dimensional world model gives an AI a more consistent understanding of space. If I move a camera, an object should remain in the same place, with the same shape. That sounds obvious to us, but it’s an important capability for a model to learn.

And once you have that representation, you can do more than reconstruct what a camera has already seen. You can explore different viewpoints, simulate movement, and ask what might happen if an agent takes a particular action. That’s useful for robotics and autonomous driving, where the system needs to understand how its actions affect the world.

But reconstruction alone is only part of the goal. The world moves, objects interact, and some things are hidden. So I see three-dimensional reconstruction as a foundation for models that can eventually predict and simulate those changes.
